summary: Folic acid is the synthetic, fully oxidised form of vitamin B9 used to treat and prevent folate-deficiency megaloblastic anaemia (sprue, nutritional, pregnancy, infancy) and to prevent neural tube defects periconceptually. Doses above 0.1 mg/day should not be used until B12 deficiency is excluded or treated, because folate corrects the anaemia of pernicious anaemia while neurologic damage progresses. Daily doses above 1 mg do not add haematologic benefit.
indications: Treatment of megaloblastic anaemia due to folic acid deficiency (e.g. tropical/non-tropical sprue)
Anaemias of nutritional origin, pregnancy, infancy or childhood
Prophylaxis of folate deficiency in pregnancy and during lactation
Periconceptional prevention of neural tube defects (per public-health guidance)

dosage.d: Up to 1 mg once daily until haematologic response; maintenance 0.4 mg/day
dosage.n: Doses >1 mg/day give no extra haematologic benefit

dosage.c: High-risk pregnancy (prior NTD, diabetes, on antiepileptics)
dosage.d: 4-5 mg daily from before conception through first trimester

dosage.n: Oral folic acid is absorbed even when food folate is not

dosage.d: Infants 0.1 mg/day; children up to 1 mg/day

admin: Oral administration is preferred and effective even in malabsorption
Parenteral route reserved for patients on parenteral/enteral nutrition
Exclude or treat vitamin B12 deficiency before using doses >0.1 mg/day
May be taken with or without food
moa: Folic acid is reduced in the body to tetrahydrofolate, a coenzyme that carries one-carbon units for synthesis of purines, thymidylate and DNA, and for methionine regeneration. Adequate folate is required for normal erythropoiesis and rapid cell division; deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and produces megaloblastic anaemia and, periconceptually, neural tube defects.

relative: Undiagnosed macrocytic anaemia until B12 deficiency excluded
Pernicious anaemia (folate alone is improper therapy)
monitor: Neurologic symptoms if B12 deficiency possible

preg: Recommended in pregnancy; periconceptional supplementation reduces the risk of neural tube defects. Higher doses (4-5 mg) are advised in women with a prior affected pregnancy or other risk factors.
lact: Folate is a normal component of breast milk and supplementation is considered safe during lactation.
renal: No routine dose adjustment. Folate is removed by dialysis, so supplementation is commonly given to patients on haemodialysis.

major: Methotrexate and other folate antagonists (trimethoprim, pyrimethamine) - folic acid may reduce antifolate efficacy; folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue is used for methotrexate toxicity
moderate: Phenytoin / phenobarbital / primidone - folic acid can lower antiepileptic levels and reduce seizure control; antiepileptics also lower folate
minor: Oral contraceptives - may modestly lower folate status
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; a folate-rich diet complements therapy.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol impairs folate absorption and increases requirement; limit intake.
interactions.diagnostics: Corrects megaloblastic indices; can mask the haematologic signs of B12 deficiency on CBC.

monitoring: CBC and reticulocyte count to confirm haematologic response
Serum vitamin B12 before treating macrocytic anaemia
Folate level where deficiency is uncertain
Neurologic status if B12 deficiency cannot be excluded
counsel: Take your dose regularly; it may be taken with or without food
In pregnancy, continue as advised to protect the baby's spine and brain development
Tell your doctor if you have pernicious anaemia or take methotrexate or epilepsy medicines
Folic acid is generally very safe; report any rash, itching or breathing difficulty
pk: Haematologic response (reticulocytosis) within a few days
Plasma peak ~1 hour after an oral dose
Hours for plasma folate; body stores last weeks to months
Daily dosing; excess >1 mg excreted unchanged in urine
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light
pearls: Never treat macrocytic anaemia with folate alone until B12 deficiency is excluded - it corrects anaemia but lets neurologic B12 damage progress
Doses above 1 mg/day add no haematologic benefit
4-5 mg/day for women with prior neural tube defect or on antiepileptics/with diabetes
Oral folic acid is absorbed even when dietary (food) folate is not
Folinic acid (leucovorin), not folic acid, is used for methotrexate rescue
missed: Take the missed dose when you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your normal schedule - do not double up.
overdose: Folic acid is relatively non-toxic; excess is excreted in the urine. The main concern is masking B12 deficiency rather than direct toxicity. Treatment is supportive.
